name: Phentermine/Topiramate (Qsymia)

lead: Qsymia pairs phentermine, a stimulant appetite suppressant, with topiramate, an anticonvulsant, in a single daily capsule. It was approved in 2012 and extended to adolescents in 2022.
Phase 3 trials show more weight loss than placebo, but newer injectable drugs outperform it in comparative analyses.

paras: Phentermine raises norepinephrine release to reduce hunger, while topiramate is thought to add satiety and reduce appetite through other brain pathways. Together they are designed to lower appetite more than either alone.
Reported effects include tingling, dry mouth, constipation, insomnia and cognitive slowing, and increased heart rate. Topiramate in pregnancy is associated with oral clefts. Prescription-only.

lead: Phentermine/topiramate extended-release (Qsymia) is a fixed-dose capsule combining phentermine, a sympathomimetic amine, with topiramate, an anticonvulsant, taken once daily to reduce appetite and increase satiety [1]. It was approved by the US FDA in 2012 for chronic weight management and in July 2022 became the first approved for pediatric use of this combination, as noted in a review of that approval [2][1]. The marketer cited in that review is VIVUS [1].

Reviews describe it as one of the more effective of the older oral obesity drugs, although network meta-analyses of drugs place incretin-based injections ahead of it [3][4][5][6]. Studies have also examined it in binge-eating disorder and bulimia, adolescents and after bariatric surgery [7][8][9].
Topiramate is associated with birth defects and the combination is reviewed for use in women of reproductive age with obesity [10].

paras: Qsymia is indicated for chronic weight management as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet and physical activity in adults with obesity or overweight with comorbidity, and since 2022 for adolescents aged 12 and older [11][1]. Developers have also pursued sleep apnoea, type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease [1].
Appearance relevance is limited to weight loss. It is discussed in reviews of obesity drugs as an option producing substantial but not bariatric-surgery-scale weight loss [12][13].

Phase 3 development included trials of controlled-release phentermine plus topiramate in overweight and obese adults; reviews summarize these as showing greater weight loss than placebo, with dose-related effects [3][4][5][11]. Smaller studies include a crossover randomized trial in binge-eating disorder and bulimia nervosa [7], a pilot in binge-eating disorder [14], a study of kidney function [15], a phase 4 study in 232 obese patients [16], a trial among wearable-tracker users [17], and studies in adolescents [8][18][19]. A trial as an adjunct to surgery in the superobese was also registered [9]. Pharmacokinetic work covers hepatic impairment [20].

Reviews and the approval record discuss paresthesia, dry mouth, constipation, insomnia and cognitive effects, as well as increased heart rate [3][4][11]. Topiramate use in pregnancy is associated with oral clefts, and reproductive-age reviews address the combination's contraception requirements [10]. Phentermine's own cardiovascular warnings are described on its article page.

The combination is designed to decrease appetite and increase satiety through two mechanisms, with phentermine acting as a sympathomimetic and topiramate acting on several neural targets [1][4]. Pharmacodynamic studies in obese patients have examined peripheral effects [21].
The combination was developed as VI-0521 and Qnexa before approval in 2012 [2][1][15]. The 2022 approval for pediatric patients followed [1].

timeline.event: First pediatric approval of the combination [1]
